answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This one is genuinely his. Wikiquote’s sourced section ↗ places the sentence on page 218 of Cosmos (New York: Random House, 1980) — and not in the “Misattributed” list further down the same page. The same apple-pie demonstration also opens the ninth episode of the companion PBS series.

source.excerpt: If you wish to make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced “Cosmos (1980)” section, cited to page 218, under a full book citation naming Random House, New York, 1980, ISBN 0394502949 and LCCN 80005286. It is absent from the same page’s “Misattributed” section, which does list several other Sagan quotes.

The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for the scanned copy ↗ confirms that edition exactly: Cosmos, 1st ed., New York: Random House, 1980, English, ISBN 0394502949, LCCN 80005286 — with a chapter list whose ninth entry is “Lives of the stars.”

Wikipedia’s article on Cosmos: A Personal Voyage ↗ dates episode 9, “The Lives of the Stars,” to 23 November 1980 and describes it opening by extrapolating the simple act of making an apple pie into the atoms and subatomic particles it requires.
Quote Investigator has never examined this line: a site search for “apple pie from scratch” ↗ returns nothing at all. Nobody has needed to debunk it.
source.excerptNote: Wikiquote records the sentence as a standalone line at page 218 without surrounding text, so only the sentence itself is reproduced here — Cosmos remains in copyright. The book’s thirteen chapters run in the same order as the thirteen episodes, and the ninth of them is “Lives of the stars”; its televised counterpart is the one that opens on an apple pie.

author.name: Carl Sagan
author.heading: Who was Carl Sagan?
author.metaLine: 1934–1996 · American astronomer, planetary scientist & science communicator
author.bio: Carl Sagan was the David Duncan Professor of Astronomy and Space Sciences at Cornell, where he directed the Laboratory for Planetary Studies, and the most recognisable scientist of his generation. His thirteen-part PBS series Cosmos: A Personal Voyage reached an audience Wikipedia puts at some 500 million people across 60 countries, and its companion book spent 70 weeks on the New York Times best-seller list. He also created the Pioneer plaque and the Voyager Golden Record — humanity’s messages to whoever might one day find them.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: This quote is real, which makes it unusual company on this site. The trouble is not who said it but how it travels — the wording drifts a word at a time, and the source keeps getting pinned to the wrong Cosmos.

items.why: The sourced text says invent, not create: Wikiquote’s page-218 citation ↗ reads “you must first invent the universe.” Shortened forms that drop “If you wish to” or swap “make” for “bake” circulate widely too. The meaning survives all of it, but ‘invent’ is the word Sagan chose, and it is the sharper one — it makes the universe sound like a piece of engineering you would have to work out first.

items.who: Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey / Neil deGrasse Tyson
items.why: The 2014 reboot shares the title, so the line sometimes gets hung on it. It predates that series by decades — Sagan’s Cosmos ran on PBS from 28 September to 21 December 1980 ↗ — and the line appears on neither Wikiquote’s Neil deGrasse Tyson page ↗ nor its Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey page ↗.

items.who: “It’s from the book” vs “it’s from the show”
items.why: Both are defensible, and the book is the citable one. Wikiquote ↗ pins the sentence to page 218 of the book, while the apple-pie demonstration is also a scene in the series — Wikipedia’s Carl Sagan article ↗ describes him cutting up an apple pie on camera in a Cambridge dining room to make a point about matter. Cite the book if you want a page number.

misattribution.truthLine: Sagan wrote it, and it is on the page: Cosmos, New York: Random House, 1980, page 218 ↗ — “If you wish to make an apple pie from scratch, you must first invent the universe.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: It is a joke with a physics lesson hidden inside it. “From scratch” in a kitchen means flour instead of a shop-bought crust; Sagan takes the phrase at its word and pushes it all the way down. A pie made truly from scratch needs carbon and oxygen and iron, and none of those were on the ingredients list at the beginning of time. They were manufactured inside stars, and released when those stars died.

That is the argument of the ninth episode of Cosmos. Wikipedia’s summary of “The Lives of the Stars” has it opening on exactly that extrapolation — a pie taken apart into atoms and subatomic particles — before turning to red giants, supernovae, white dwarfs, neutron stars, pulsars and black holes. The apple pie is the hook; stellar nucleosynthesis is the point. It is Sagan’s whole method in one sentence: start in a kitchen, end at the origin of matter, and never once make the listener feel stupid.
context.detailsSummary: How the book and the series fit together
detailsBody: The book was not adapted from the series so much as built alongside it, and its thirteen chapters run in the same order as the thirteen broadcasts. The Internet Archive’s catalogue record for the first edition ↗ lists them, from “Shores of the cosmic ocean” through “Lives of the stars” to “Who speaks for Earth?” — the same closing title PBS broadcast on 21 December 1980.

It worked on a scale science broadcasting had not seen. The companion volume ↗ spent 70 weeks on the New York Times best-seller list and sold in the millions, and the series ↗ won Emmy and Peabody awards. Which is why a throwaway line about dessert is now one of the most quoted sentences in popular science.
context.pull: A pie made truly from scratch needs carbon, oxygen and iron — and none of those existed until stars made them.
